questions.prompt: About how heavy would a teaspoon of white-dwarf matter be on your kitchen scale?
options: A few grams, like sugar
A few kilograms, like a laptop
About five and a half tons — like a school bus
It would float, so almost nothing
questions.explanation: A white dwarf packs between half and 1.4 solar masses into a ball the size of Earth. Squeezed into a teaspoon, that matter weighs roughly 5.5 tons.
questions.misconception: Everything you have ever touched is ordinary matter, so a star's leftover does not sound denser than granite — but here the particles are nearly touching, about a million times denser than anything on Earth.

questions.prompt: What stops a white dwarf from collapsing under its own gravity?
options: Fusion in its core keeps it hot
Electron degeneracy pressure — electrons refuse to be squeezed closer together
A magnetic field cradles the star
Rotation so fast it would fly apart
questions.explanation: Quantum rules forbid two electrons from sharing the same place. As gravity compresses them, that refusal creates a pressure that does not depend on temperature — so the star is held open even though nothing is burning.
questions.misconception: After the red giant, 'the core burns' is the easy guess — but this object has no furnace at all; what props it up is electron refusal, not fire.

questions.prompt: How is a white dwarf born?
options: A newborn star starts out as a white dwarf
A red giant sheds its outer envelope, leaving its core exposed
A planet reheats until it turns white
Two stars merge and then freeze
questions.explanation: The red giant's weak outer layers drift off as a planetary nebula, and the exposed, super-dense core is the white dwarf — this scene is written all over the sky.
questions.misconception: A 'planetary nebula' sounds like it should make planets, and a glowing leftover sounds like a newborn star — but the name is a historical accident, and the dwarf is at the end of a star's life, not the beginning.

questions.prompt: A white dwarf glows white-hot but is not fusing anything. Why does it still shine?
options: It reflects light from nearby stars
It is radiating away its stored heat, cooling like an ember with no fire
It has a hidden nuclear glow stick
It is actually sparkling liquid
questions.explanation: When fusion stops, the dwarf keeps the enormous heat earned during its lifetime. That heat leaks away over billions of years, so it glows, then cools — it never re-lights.
questions.misconception: White-hot naturally suggests something is burning, but the dwarf is a stove after the fuel line was cut: still warm, but no new heat is being made.

questions.prompt: What happens if a white dwarf is pushed past the Chandrasekhar limit (about 1.4 solar masses)?
options: Nothing special — it quietly gets heavier forever
Electron pressure can no longer hold it; it must become something denser or blow up
It turns into a planet
It suddenly starts fusing again like a fresh star
questions.explanation: Above ~1.4 solar masses even electron degeneracy gives out, and the core either collapses into a neutron star or — in a binary pair — explodes as a type Ia supernova. The white dwarf cannot just keep growing.
questions.misconception: Adding mass sounds harmless, but quantum pressure has a hard maximum; at the limit the standoff collapses instead of adjusting.
